evidence.title: Unstoppable? LLMs analysing stylized strategic decision problems in the social sciences
evidence.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has made amazing progress in recent years. Today’s computers play complex board games such as chess and Go far above the level of human world champions. Widely available AI models can also sustain human-like conversations and pass the Turing test (Biever et al. 2023). Most impressively, DeepMind’s AlphaFold has solved open scientific research problems, for example, a ‘50-year challenge’ concerning protein folding, which earned the 2024 Nobel prize in Chemistry for its human developers. The purpose of this study is to establish whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can analyse stylized strategic decision problems in the social sciences. The problem sets that we use originate from undergraduate PPE admission interview passages at Jesus College, Oxford. Each standardized problem sheet consists of a preamble (setup) and five questions that examine societal issues such as conflicts between individual incentives and group objectives, tensions between commitment and sequential rationality, and problems arising from asymmetric information. Most of these exercises are game-theoretic in nature, presented verbally, without mathematical formalism. Some are based on known paradoxes, others on more recently published theoretical research, but the problem sheets themselves have not been published before. The problem sheets that we use are in Appendix C, their solutions in Appendix E. Within each problem, some of the questions are purely quantitative (e.g., asking for a computation of certain quantities or probabilities based on assumptions made in the setup); others intend to elicit insights that require a more thorough understanding of the situation and of how humans would behave. (The categorization of questions is in Appendix D.) We test five off-the-shelf LLMs available in early 2025: ChatGPT o3, Claude, Grok 3, Llama, and Gemini. The mathematical and scientific problem-solving capabilities of AI systems have been the subject of much recent research. Williams (2024) reports that DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 solved four out of six problems in the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, equivalent to a Silver Medal for human competitors. But there are limitations. FrontierMath, a collection of 300 difficult, unpublished problems developed by researchers at Epoch AI, is used to benchmark the limits of AI in mathematical problem-solving. At the time of writing, only about 9% of FrontierMath’s problems can be solved by state-of-the-art AI systems, although the proportion is rising (it was 2% in December 2024; see Glazer et al. 2024). Another recent example is Humanity’s Last Exam, set up by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI (Phan et al. 2025). This comprises 3,000 brief but challenging questions deliberately designed to push the limits of modern AI systems, with 84% of its problems drawn from STEM fields. Most of today’s AI systems perform poorly on these questions, although accuracy rates vary across models. There is also substantial heterogeneity, for example, AI struggles more with combinatorics than geometry (Trinh et al. 2024), suggesting that humans still have comparative advantages in certain types of reasoning. In addition, AI systems appear to be making rapid progress in their usefulness for social science research in many respects. Recent studies (e.g., Aher, Arriaga, and Kalai, 2023) find that GPT models can simulate human subjects and replicate classical findings in various game-theoretic experiments commonly cited in the social sciences. This suggests that AI models may one day partially replace human participants in social science experiments, generating synthetic data to test ideas at a lower cost and with less demand on human subjects (Bail 2024; Grossman et al. 2024, although see Rossi et al. 2024 for a critique). Yet while it seems that AI can act as a subject in social science research, it remains to be seen whether AI can act as a social scientist. Our focus is on the latter, by testing whether LLMs, available as of early 2025, can analyse human behaviour as a social scientist would, rather than acting as research participants. We therefore focus on stylized strategic decision problems with applications in the social sciences. title: Cross-Domain Transfer Performance of Tabular Foundation Models Pretrained on Synthetic Adversarial Data Versus Real-World Datasets
abstract: The development of tabular foundation models (TFMs) has accelerated in recent years, showing strong potential to outperform traditional ML methods for structured data. title: Causal Synthetic Data Generation for Robust Tabular Foundation Models Under Cross-Domain Distribution Shifts
abstract: Fine-tuning tabular foundation models (TFMs) under data scarcity is challenging, as early stopping on even scarcer validation data often fails to capture true generalization performance. We propose CausalMixFT, a method that enhances fine-tuning robustness and downstream performance by generating structurally consistent synthetic samples using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) fitted on the target dataset. This approach augments limited real data with causally informed synthetic examples, preserving feature dependencies while expanding training diversity. Evaluated across 33 classification datas Research goal: Can causal synthetic data generation improve the robustness of tabular foundation models against distribution shifts in cross-domain evaluation settings relative to non-causal methods? title: Transcript Binding Failure in Fiat-Shamir Decryption Proofs: A Case Study in Swiss Post E-Voting Infrastructure
abstract: We report a transcript binding failure in the Fiat-Shamir challenge construction of the DecryptionProofService component within the Swiss Post e-voting cryptographic primitives library (crypto-primitives v1.5.2.1). The vulnerability arises because the Fiat-Shamir auxiliary transcript omits the gamma component of the ElGamal ciphertext during challenge derivation. Since the challenge hash is computed over (phi, m) rather than the complete ciphertext (gamma, phi, m), a proof generated for one ciphertext may verify successfully against a distinct ciphertext sharing the same phi and plaintext m but with a different gamma. We demonstrate this class of weakness through proof-of-concept analysis, characterise the cryptographic conditions under which it manifests, assess the practical security implications for verifiable election systems, and propose a minimal one-line remediation. The finding was responsibly disclosed to the Swiss Post security team on March 10, 2026 under report YWH-R879012.

title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Marketing Performance: An Empirical Investigation from Indian Firms
abstract: This study empirically examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on marketing performance among Indian firms. Drawing on the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Dynamic Capabilities theory, the study develops and tests a conceptual model encompassing four AI-enabled marketing dimensions—AI-Driven Customer Analytics (AICA), Marketing Automation (MA), Personalisation Capability (PC), and Predictive Lead Scoring (PLS)—as antecedents of marketing performance, with Customer Engagement (CE) as a mediator and Firm Innovativeness (FI) as a moderator. Data were collected from 390 marketing professionals across six industry sectors using a structured questionnaire. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) with AMOS 24 was employed for hypothesis testing, supplemented by bootstrapped mediation analysis (5,000 resamples). All four AI dimensions demonstrated significant positive effects on marketing performance. Customer engagement mediated the AI–performance relationship, while firm innovativeness positively moderated the AICA–performance link. The findings provide actionable insights for marketing managers and contribute to the nascent empirical literature on AI-driven marketing in emerging market contexts.

title: SIGACT News Complexity Theory Column 129 Compressing Correlated Randomness
abstract: Is it possible to emulate sampling from an arbitrary efficiently-samplable distribution using an efficient deterministic procedure which is initially fed with a short random seed and increments a counter after each query? Yes, under minimal cryptographic assumptions (the existence of one-way functions) as shown by a sequence of celebrated results in the 80s. Equivalently, one can view this problem as the goal to compress a large number of (seemingly) random samples into a short random seed. But what happens when multiple parties want, given short correlated random seeds distributed in a one-time initialization step, to deterministically and non-interactively obtain correlated samples that cannot be distinguished (even by a subset of the participants themselves) from random samples from a joint distribution? In other words, can cryptography help us compress (seemingly) random correlated samples? Our knowledge of this natural generalization of the problem is considerably more limited, and there is much more that we don't know than we know! Nevertheless, many special cases of this question have been explored in recent (and not so recent) works, motivated in part by numerous applications to other cryptographic tasks. In this article, I provide an introductory exposition of the topic, recasting a number of results originally introduced using various formalisms, under the lens of compressed samplers for multiple parties.

title: Bridging the synthetic-to-real domain gap with network dissection analysis
abstract: Synthetic data plays a significant role in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) applications, especially for Aided Target Recognition (AiTR). Domains with sparse data can be significantly supplemented with the addition of data generated through various methods, such as physics-based simulators, game engine rendering, and generative AI. However, the synthetic-to-real domain gap problem persists, such that synthetic datasets alone differ from real datasets when used in AiTR applications. This can be attributed to a number of factors, largely consisting of three major gaps in dataset distribution, realism, and labeling. The realism gap encompasses differences that cause a statistical difference between synthetic and real imagery such that synthetic data does not adequately capture features of real-world imagery used by neural networks for positive target identification. These features can include subtle variations in texture, lighting, and digital artifacts. A significant amount of ork has been conducted to reduce the synthetic-to-real performance domain gap through various methods, such as domain randomization and domain adaptation. These approaches try to statistically capture differences through trial and error or through other AI methods. Alternatively, this work explores the use of network dissection to identify concepts used by neural networks for target identification, which are beneficial to characterize differences between synthetic and real Infrared (IR) imagery that can be modified to improve AiTR performance. This targeted approach explores a method to identify and understand specific concepts associated with different neural network responses between synthetic and real imagery to target specific changes that bridge the domain gap. We present results showing that identified concepts that negatively influence AiTR can be used to generate new synthetic datasets that improve model performance.

title: Regulatory requirement classification and semantic verification for model-based ship design
abstract: Maritime regulations define constraints on ship design spanning areas such as structural safety, environmental emissions, and lifecycle requirements. This paper proposes a method for classifying regulatory requirements by verification type and encoding them as machine-executable constraints over a semantic model built with the Web Ontology Language (OWL), the Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) and SPARQL. Each regulatory clause is assigned to one of five categories — Static, Static Calculation, Dynamic, Complex, and Physical Test — based on their verification type. SHACL shapes for directly verifiable categories validate parameter values and computed quantities against regulatory constraints. For regulations requiring simulation-driven verification, the model is first validated for the variables and component relationships the simulation requires before the simulation can proceed. Physical verification processes are tracked by explicit status in the same semantic model. To validate the approach, 201 requirements from the Finnish-Swedish Ice Class Rules published by TRAFICOM are formalized, and verification against independently published sample ship data resolves 50 requirements to passed status, while the remaining 151 are traceable to specific design parameters not yet available in the model. The approach transforms the regulatory text into active constraints on the design model, providing engineers with reliable compliance management as the regulatory complexity grows.

title: Scalable Deep Unfolding of Conic Optimizers
abstract: Deep unfolding (DU) accelerates iterative optimizers by introducing learnable components and training them through unrolled iterations, but extending DU to the large-scale semidefinite programs (SDPs) common in robotics has remained limited. Unrolling a full-update conic solver such as COSMO exposes two obstacles that prior work on learned conic solvers has not: backpropagating through the per-iteration linear-system solve incurs memory quadratic in the problem size once the coefficient matrix is formed explicitly, and backpropagating through the positive semidefinite (PSD) cone projection becomes numerically unstable when eigenvalues coincide. We address the first obstacle with a matrix-free implicit differentiation rule that operates entirely through matrix-vector products, reducing memory from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ and enabling backpropagation at scales where direct factorization runs out of memory. We address the second with a backward rule based on the Dalečkii--Krein representation of the Fréchet derivative, which remains well-defined under repeated eigenvalues. Together these make it possible to learn lightweight hyperparameter policies and warm-starts for a full-update conic solver. We evaluate on nonlinear covariance steering problems solved via sequential convex programming (SCP), as well as standalone SDPs and second-order cone programs ranging from max-cut and Lovász $\vartheta$ SDPs to robust estimation and control problems. The learned policies outperform state-of-the-art solvers across all problems, and can provide up to a 50$\times$ speedup depending on the class. When used as a subroutine in SCP, the learned approach delivers over a 30$\times$ speedup compared to COSMO.
